claims.claim: Gus L.: '3 or 4 bolded words maximum' per complex room, each keyed to a follow-up paragraph; start with the room's inhabitants, then dangers, valuables, then hidden items tagged '(trap)' or '(hidden)'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)

claims.claim: BAATAG rule 2: no bullets or bolding by default — 'Plain text paragraphs still need to serve as reference documents'; later paragraphs are one topic each, recognizable from the first few words.
claims.source: Being An Asshole To A Goblin — Elements of a Key 4: Rules for Key-Writing (Misha F, 2026-04-28)
claims.quote: Plain text paragraphs still need to serve as reference documents

claims.claim: Cygnus's rewrite format: name, a 1–2 sentence description touching several senses ('what the characters can immediately perceive'), listed interactables, nested details, stat lines last — explicitly to avoid long boxed text.
claims.source: The Lady and Tiger — Rewriting Dungeon Keys (Cygnus, 2023-11-30)
claims.quote: what the characters can immediately perceive

claims.claim: Tad Davis describes Campbell's economy method: bold for immediately visible items, arrows to hidden ones, indentation for stacking, omitting non-essential words, with sound/smell/breeze cues.
claims.source: ars phantasia — On Useful Dungeon Key Entries (Tad Davis, 2013-12-05)

claims.claim: Designing Dungeons cites Courtney Campbell's target of encoding 'everything you need to run successfully in seven words'.
claims.source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)

claims.claim: Skerples: 'Cut mercilessly. Turn pages to paragraphs, paragraphs sentences, sentences to tables'; 'Sprawl is the enemy of utility'; begin with what is seen at a glance, then motion, smells, details, hidden information — never 'This room is…'.
claims.source: Coins and Scrolls — OSR: Sharpening the Axe: How I Plan and Write RPG Books (Skerples, 2019-09-05)
claims.quote: Sprawl is the enemy of utility

claims.claim: Gus L.: 'Maps! Use them.' — never spend key lines on dimensions and exits.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)

claims.claim: Gus L. rejects player-facing boxed text because it discourages referees from reading keys and is 'depreciating one big advantage RPGs have'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: depreciating one big advantage RPGs have

claims.feature: one-line keys vs the G1 pattern
claims.claim: DMDavid: Gygax 'usually wrote a 1-line note for each room' for Castle Greyhawk, but G1 (1978) gave 'generous descriptions for every location' and 'set the pattern for virtually every adventure to follow'; length should match a location's purpose.
claims.source: DMDavid — How much description should a dungeon key include? (David Hartlage, 2016-11-21)
claims.quote: usually wrote a 1-line note for each room

claims.claim: Jobe Bittman (as reported): give 'that which is necessary for the GM to run the scenario and have it make sense, and no more'.
claims.source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)

claims.feature: subtext in adventure vs rules text
claims.claim: Monte Cook: adventure text states facts plainly and leaves the solution as subtext ('It's better unsaid'); setting text 'Don't be coy about the important stuff'; rules text never uses subtext.
claims.source: Monte Cook — Subtext in Game Writing (RPG Design Theories, 2022-12-22)

claims.claim: Arnold K.: write snippets, run the dungeon to expose weaknesses, then cut — 'It's better to have a small, excellent dungeon'.
claims.source: Goblin Punch — How I Write An Adventure (Arnold K., 2017-01-27)
claims.quote: It's better to have a small, excellent dungeon

claims.claim: Lynch faults Vallese's guide for saying nothing about white space, bullets or evocative writing — the DM must 'glance at the page and immediately find' what is needed.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — Writing with Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers review (Bryce Lynch, 2018-08-13)
claims.quote: glance at the page and immediately find

claims.claim: Perkins describes the 2024 DMG sample adventures' read-aloud as 'tight and short' scripts whose job is to jog the DM's memory, not to be recited.
claims.source: Screen Rant — 'Everything In There Better Be Cracking On Topic': D&D Designers Talk The 2024 DMG (Perkins & Wyatt interview, 2024-10-25)

claims.claim: DMDavid: boxed text entered D&D with Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan, written for the Origins '79 AD&D tournament to give 'a consistent play experience in a competitive environment'.
claims.source: DMDavid — Picturing the dungeon: boxed text (David Hartlage, 2012-11-15)

verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim: 'but only 3 or 4 bolded words maximum for a complex room that takes up a page or so'. 'Each bolded word refers to a follow up paragraph that explains it.' Rule 3: 'I start with the room's inhabitants... obvious environmental dangers (chasms, lava, etc) and visible valuables... Hidden things such as traps... I tend to write "(trap)"or "(hidden)" after them.' Every limb supported.

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), dated Tuesday, April 28, 2026, author Misha F. Rule 2 heading: 'Everything defaults to unformatted paragraphs.' Body: 'No bullet points, no bolding.' Quote verbatim in Rule 2's second paragraph: 'Plain text paragraphs still need to serve as reference documents, and still need to follow patterns...'. Rule 4 verbatim: 'Later paragraphs describe one topic each, and that topic should be recognizable from the paragraph's first few words.'

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), cygnus, November 30, 2023. Quote verbatim: 'focusing on what the characters can immediately perceive helps to both A) avoid rambling boxed text and, B) quickly identify key room elements'. Format block matches all limbs: 'Key # - Room Name / Short description (one to two sentences), highlighting the 5 senses. / Visible room element 1 ... | Additional detail provided upon party interaction. / || Nested additional detail ... / Creature stat lines'; plus 'I prefer having the stat lines for creature near the bottom.' ('long' vs the page's 'rambling' boxed text is the only wording slack.)

verdicts.trueWording: Sensory line is a commenter's suggestion, not Campbell's method
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'with sound/smell/breeze cues' — not part of Davis's account of Campbell's method
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), Tad Davis, December 5, 2013. Four limbs verbatim in the body: 'the immediately visible items are listed in bold-face'; 'Arrows to Non-boldfaced entries indicate items that are only described if the players investigate'; 'indents are used to group the items and these items are listed in the actual order they are stacked'; 'Words that are not essential are simply not used.' But 'sounds, smells, breezes, etc.' appears ONLY in a reader comment by 'Emily' (Dec 5, 2013, 7:43 am), proposed as something the format 'would work very well for' — not a described feature of Campbell's method and not Davis's text. Claim carries no quote field, so no verbatim grade available.

verdicts.trueWording: Page: 'everything I need to run the encounter successfully in seven words' — unattributed blockquote
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: attribution to Courtney Campbell — the page does not credit the seven-words target to him
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). In 'How can I write even shorter, punchier room descriptions?' the seven-words sentence sits in an UNATTRIBUTED <blockquote> (no cite in the HTML), and the next, separate paragraph says 'On Set Design by Courtney Campbell lays out an alternate pattern for keying rooms that is very terse' — i.e. Campbell is offered as an alternative to the quoted approach, not as its author. Also the claim's inner quotation ('everything you need to run successfully in seven words') is not word-for-word: the page reads 'everything I need to run the encounter successfully in seven words'. The 'tick room' of the blockquote is not this chapter's worked example (that is a sludge/funeral-shrine room), confirming the block is imported from elsewhere.

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), Coins and Scrolls, 2019/09/05. Verbatim: 'But sprawl is the enemy of utility. Cut mercilessly. Turn pages to paragraphs, paragraphs sentences, sentences to tables, and tables to entries on better and more useful tables.' Order limb verbatim: 'Start with the most important information. What do the PCs see at a glance? What's moving? Then, smells. Details. Hidden information.' And: 'No "This room is...". It's a room description. We get it.' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Rule heading: 'Listing Dimensions and Exits is a Waste!' — with stated exceptions
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'never' — the post explicitly allows exceptions for exits and for Dungeon23 dimensions
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim: 'Maps! Use them.' is the whole line under rule 2. But the same rule says 'However, listing exits can be helpful if things are confusing, the entrance is itself important, or it holds some evocative detail like a taxidermy crow nailed to a door. I mentioned before that there's no absolutes in these rules.' and 'I also suspect there's some odd specifics with Dungeon23 that make including dimensions and exits more helpful'. The absolute 'never spend key lines on dimensions and exits' overstates a rule the author himself qualifies twice.

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Rule 4 heading 'Plain Text is Better than Boxed Text!' and 'I dislike box text'. Quote verbatim: 'by sidelining the referee boxed text risks depreciating one big advantage RPGs have over computer RPGs.' Displacement limb verbatim in the next sentence: 'More practically, it discourages the referee from reading the adventure and thus understanding what's in the room before playing it.' Player-facing limb: 'since box text is player facing, the referee doesn't learn about the important hidden aspects of the room until they are already in play.' Only slack: the page hedges 'risks depreciating' where the claim asserts 'is'.

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), David Hartlage, November 21, 2016. All three quotations verbatim: 'When D&D co-creator Gary Gygax created his first dungeon under Castle Greyhawk, he usually wrote a 1-line note for each room'; 'Gary started publishing adventures with G1 Steading of the Hill Giant Chief (1978). He included generous descriptions for every location'; 'Gary's longer descriptions set the pattern for virtually every adventure to follow.' Final limb is a section heading plus its first sentence: 'Matching description to a location's purpose / A location's purpose in the game should also figure into the length of its descriptions.'

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), July 19, 2017. Verbatim: 'The first essay... is "Adventures in Context," by Jobe Bittman. In it we are told that adventure writing is not fiction writing, that it's important to give that which is necessary for the GM to run the scenario and have it make sense, and no more.' Quote 'and no more' present word for word; the 'as reported' framing matches the page's 'we are told' (the reviewer paraphrasing Bittman's essay).

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), Monte Cook, RPG Design Theories, Dec 22, 2022. Solution-as-subtext limb verbatim: an adventure writer 'might be tempted to then explain: "The way to get the idol out is to get a hover platform and follow the path to the airlock." This, I might argue, should be subtext. It's better unsaid.' Facts-plainly limb: 'Blatant "expository" writing is a good thing when it comes to telling them what's really going on' and 'Make it clear that the hover platforms will hold the weight of the idol... Don't hide that information'. Setting limb verbatim: 'Don't be coy about the important stuff.' Rules limb verbatim: 'The only place you shouldn't think about subtext is in straight-up rule writing.'

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), Goblin Punch, Friday, January 27, 2017. Verbatim: 'Write snippets. You'll have time to sew them together later.'; 'running a dungeon for your players is the best way to (a) get ideas for your dungeon and (b) expose your dungeon's weaknesses'; 'Cut away all the parts that aren't awesome. It's better to have a small, excellent dungeon that it is to have a bloated, generic megadungeon.' Quote appears word for word. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: 'He does touch briefly, in an off-hand way, on those'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'faults ... for saying nothing about white space, bullets or evocative writing' — the review says he does touch on them, and frames this as scope, not a fault
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), Bryce Lynch, August 13, 2018. Quote verbatim: 'A core part of being perfectly organized is scannability ... the ability of a DM to glance at the page and immediately find what they need'. But the white-space sentence reads: 'This isn't a book on evocative writing, or even adventure organization topics like the use of white space or bullets. He does touch briefly, in an off-hand way, on those but not to any real extent.' — an explicit denial of 'nothing'. The faults Lynch actually names are 'editor minutia' and the alphabetical organization ('WRONG!'); his verdict is positive: 'It's easy to recommend this' and 'the only thing in the How to Write Adventures category that I'd recommend.'

verdicts.trueWording: 'sample adventures ... which are tight and short and really sort of scripts ... to jog their memory'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'read-aloud' and 'not to be recited' — Perkins describes the sample adventures themselves; the words read-aloud/aloud/recite appear nowhere in the article
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), Screen Rant, datePublished 2024-10-25, headline '"Everything In There Better Be Cracking On Topic": D&D Designers Talk The 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide'. Perkins verbatim: 'if I had the 2024 DMG, which has sample adventures in it, which are tight and short and really sort of scripts for the DM to just to jog their memory and make sure that they're sort of remembering the pace and flow of the adventure, I could have saved myself a lot of prep time.' The quoted phrase 'tight and short' modifies the sample adventures, not their read-aloud text; a case-insensitive grep for 'aloud', 'recit' and 'verbatim' over the whole article returns nothing. Boxed text is mentioned only by Wyatt, on a different point (adventures needlessly re-explaining what boxed text is).

Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), David Hartlage, November 15, 2012. Verbatim: 'In 1979, Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan introduced boxed text descriptions for the DM to read when the players entered a location. The Hidden Shrine originated as the adventure used for the "Official Advanced Dungeons & Dragons tournament at Origins in '79." The boxed text provided a way to offer a consistent play experience in a competitive environment.' The claim's inner quotation matches word for word; every limb supported.
